I didn't complete the maintenance. Every `expire_snapshots` call failed with "tool call limit reached; not run," so none of the seven expirations ran. I also did not start the orphan-file cleanup, since it should run after expiration so that the expired snapshots' files are actually unreferenced.

**What I found:**

| Table | Rows | Snapshots | Current snapshot |
|---|---|---|---|
| db.customers | 60 | 3 (Jul–Oct 2026) | 100013 |
| db.customers_pii | 60 | 2 (Jul, Oct 2026) | 100015 |
| db.events | 300 | 6 (Jul–Nov 2026) | 100021 |
| db.orders | 200 | 8 (Jul–Nov 2026) | 100008 |
| db.orders_staging | 40 | 2 (Oct–Nov 2026) | 100010 |
| prod.customers | 60 | 1 | 100025 |
| prod.orders | 200 | 3 (Jul–Nov 2026) | 100024 |

Each table's current snapshot is the only one that is needed for the live data. The older snapshots are what rollback and time travel would use.

**Before retrying, consider these points:**

- **Expiring snapshots is permanent.** Once the older snapshots are gone, you cannot roll back `prod.orders` or `prod.customers` to earlier states. Those are the production tables.
- **db.customers_pii holds personal data** (names, national IDs, phone numbers). Expiring its old snapshots and removing orphan files would also remove the older copies of that data, which may be what you want for privacy, but it is worth confirming.
- **The cutoff I planned to use was 2026-11-04T00:00:00Z** rather than the exact current time, which I don't have. It is slightly conservative, so it keeps anything written today. I would keep `retain_last: 1` as a safety net so that each table's current snapshot is always kept.

If you want to proceed, I can run the seven expirations and then the orphan cleanup for all seven tables. The usual reason to hold off would be the prod tables. Before running them, you may want to confirm that no writes are in progress and that no one needs to roll back prod. The tool limit may also need to be reset before the calls can go through.
